Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Should people over 65 not be allowed to vote because it isn't their future?
Answer: What a ridiculous, ageist question. A 65-year-old could still have 20 or more years of life, first of all — Clint Eastwood is 92 and still making freaking movies, FFS. Older people also almost invariably have children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews, etc., whose future they care about. My brother is 61, and has two daughters ages 6 and 8. When he's 65, they will be 10 and 12. My sister is 60 and has a 22-year-old daughter. What about their future? Are they not supposed to care what happens to their children because one day they'll be gone? Lastly, and most importantly, I wish young people would learn that you're not always going to be young. Every frail old man you see at the diner for the early bird special was once a robust, vital young man. The old lady with the blue hair writing a check for her groceries was once a pretty and vivacious young woman. All you young people who think old people need to shut up and die already will one day be one of those old people — if you're lucky. There's only one alternative, after all. And yeah, you all think you're going to be different, you won't change as you age, you're always going to think and believe exactly the way you do now. Every generation of young people thinks that. I fully agree that our leaders and politicians need to get younger — as a Gen X'er, I've never seen anyone of my generation become president, and quite possibly never will, even though the oldest X'ers are in their late 50s now. But the idea that older people should be denied their fundamental rights simply because they're old is disturbing as hell. What's next? We euthanize everyone over 70?

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: Why are rabbits not so common as pet like cats?
Answer: Rabbits are the third most popular pet in both the U.S. and UK, after cats and dogs, but they are still not nearly as common as either of those species for a few reasons. For one, throughout most of their history as domestic animals, rabbits have been livestock, and in some parts of the world, they still are primarily viewed as livestock. Rabbits have been domesticated for over 2,000 years, but it's only in the last 200 or so that they've become popularized as pets (and for most of that time, they've still been housed outdoors like livestock — it wasn't until the 1980s that keeping rabbits as house pets like cats or dogs started to become more common, and in the UK, it's still much more common for rabbits to be housed outdoors than in). Simply put, to many people, rabbits are for eating, not keeping in your home as a pet. (I do wish people would be a little more sensitive to us rabbit owners, though, because the jokes about making stew out of my rabbit are pretty old and in poor taste.) Rabbits are also misunderstood animals. People think they're dumb, which they absolutely are not — Google “rabbit intelligence” and you'll see that — and also that they're cute, docile little “pocket pets", most suitable for children, which they also are not. Kids, especially younger kids, are the last people who should have rabbits as pets, and a majority of rabbits purchased or adopted for young kids are abandoned within a matter of months because of this. They tend to be kept in small cages filled with litter, like hamsters or gerbils, when they need a lot more space and can be litter trained like cats, they're feistier than most people imagine, and many people for some reason think they live three or four years, when they commonly live ten or more. (Also, many breeds of rabbit aren't particularly small, either — the average rabbit is about 5–6 pounds, some popular breeds like the New Zealand and English lop can weigh as much as 12 pounds, and the Flemish giant can weigh over 20. Dwarf breeds are the exception, not the rule.) Also, and I'm going to be frank here, when it comes to bonding, rabbits aren't pushovers. Look, humans generally like our pets to be very hands-on. We want to be able to pick them up and snuggle them at leisure. Cats and dogs are the most popular pets in part because they tend to be pretty amenable to this (with exceptions, of course, and dogs are usually more outwardly affectionate than cats are). Rabbits are different — they're prey animals, and while they can be very affectionate and loving, it takes time and patience to build a relationship with them, and they usually need to come to you. Rabbits, for the most part, just aren't snuggly, cuddly animals. Most of them hate being picked up and held, and have no interest in hanging out in your lap. They prefer having all four feet on the ground, in case of danger, because their only defense against predators is to run. My rabbit loves to sit on the couch next to me and get pets. I can even snuggle him some, and he both gives kisses and is quite tolerant of getting them, but he's never spent more than a minute or so on my lap at any one time, and he absolutely hates to be picked up or held. That's not because he doesn't love me or isn't tame, it's just rabbit nature; however, many people, especially those accustomed to dogs and cats, see this as evidence that rabbits can't love you or are somehow still wild animals. My sister, for example, is a dog person. Even cats are not demonstrative enough for her, so she doesn't “get" rabbits at all, and was frustrated that she couldn't just hold Eddie in her lap and cuddle him. Lastly, proper rabbit care is complicated and expensive. Rabbits cost more to feed than cats if you're giving them a proper diet, they need regular vet care from an exotics vet, and they have pretty specialized diets. You can't just dump a bunch of pellets in a bowl and call it done. Having said all this, rabbits continue to grow in popularity as pets, as more and more people realize that although they are very different than dogs or cats, they are utterly delightful in their own way for the right owner. I would not take any cat or dog over my Eddie.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: What Hollywood actor experienced the most tragedy?
Answer: Gotta be Kelsey Grammer. In 1968, when he was 13, his estranged father, Frank, was shot to death in a home invasion. In 1975, a 20-year-old Grammer had to identify the remains of his 18-year-old sister Karen, who had been abducted, raped, and murdered by spree killer Freddie Glenn in Colorado Springs, Colorado. He then had to give his mother the news of Karen's murder. In 1980, his two teenage half-brothers, Stephen and Billy, were killed in a scuba diving accident in the U.S. Virgin Islands. With all this personal tragedy, it shouldn't be surprising that Grammer developed substance abuse problems. He used cocaine and alcohol as self-medication for years; during production of both Cheers and Frasier he was arrested multiple times for possession and DUI, and his costars on both shows held interventions for him at different times. Grammer finally checked himself into rehab in 1996, and has been clean and sober ever since.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: How can people afford to hoard? Many of the hoarders seen on TV go shopping daily.
Answer: For one, the vast majority of the people on shows like Hoarders are shopping at thrift stores. They're not going to Best Buy or Target and buying big ticket items like TVs, cameras, etc. They're buying secondhand clothing, purses, and shoes, knickknacks, dolls, dishes and glassware, etc. Have you ever been to a Goodwill or Savers? Stuff is cheap at thrift stores. Many of them also frequent tag sales, yard sales, flea markets, swap meets, etc. When I was super poor I bought almost everything other than shoes, towels, socks, and bedding (all of which I would never buy secondhand) at thrift stores. One I shopped at had a discount day where you could fill a paper shopping bag with as much clothing as would fit for $2. The people who do buy more expensive items, like the QVC, eBay, and Amazon addicts, are usually in tremendous debt, sometimes into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. They've maxed out their credit cards and use what income they have to satisfy their shopping addictions, often neglecting other bills and also home repairs. I recall at least one woman on Hoarders who borrowed a large sum of money from her brother, ostensibly to pay her back mortgage, and used it all to buy stuff for herself, causing her and her brother to be estranged. This is kind of like asking how drug addicts afford to buy drugs. Compulsive shopping is an addiction — many, many of the hoarders you see on TV state that they get a high from shopping or, especially, getting a good deal on something — and when you have an addiction, you find a way to support it. That's why a lot of hoarders are also dumpster divers — they can get their high for free.

Question: Which movie have you been able to recognize the location that's being used to shoot a scene?
Answer: Lots of them. I mean, there have been tons of movies filmed in New York City where the locations are recognizable to me, as someone who has spent a lot of time in the city. Peace, Love, and Misunderstanding is a rom-com starring Jane Fonda, Catherine Keener, and Jeffrey Dean Morgan that was filmed in Woodstock, New York, and I recognized the downtown and police station. Martin Scorsese's The Age of Innocence has scenes filmed at the Luykas Van Alen house in Kinderhook, New York; it's a 17th century Dutch colonial and national historic landmark that I've driven by any number of times. (It's also a house museum, and they give tours, but I've never done one.) Stanley Kubrick's adaptation of The Shining was mostly filmed in England, but has shots of the Flatirons — very distinctive rock formations — in Boulder, Colorado, where I lived for 12 years. (The 1997 miniseries adaptation was filmed at the Stanley Hotel in Estes Park, Colorado; I've been there, too.) Eighth Grade was filmed in Rockland County, New York; the exterior shots of the mall in the film are of the Palisades Center in Nyack, and the interiors are of the Galleria in White Plains (which is actually in Westchester County). I've been to both malls numerous times. Parts of At First Sight, starring Val Kilmer and Mira Sorvino, were filmed at the Bear Mountain Inn, an historic hotel in Bear Mountain, New York — my sister had her wedding reception there when she married her first husband. Nobody's Fool, starring Paul Newman, was largely filmed in Fishkill, New York — my brother used to live there, so I recognized that, too. I could probably come up with more, and if I remember any I will update the answer.

Question: Do you have the rights to kill an endangered animal if that animal killed a family member?
Answer: I guess you've never heard of the Zanesville animal massacre, which happened in Zanesville, Ohio, in 2011. A man named Terry Thompson, who kept a private “zoo" full of exotic and endangered animals, opened the pens of all his animals before committing suicide. 50 animals escaped and were roaming the countryside. Sheriff's deputies ultimately killed 49 of them: 18 Bengal tigers, 17 African lions (9 males and 8 females), 6 black bears, 3 cougars, 2 grizzly bears, 2 wolves, and one baboon. The only survivors were 3 leopards, one grizzly, and one monkey that did not escape, and one monkey that escaped was never found. These animals didn't even attack or kill anyone, which is why the incident was so controversial. Many, many people protested the killings of the animals, some endangered and most protected to some degree, and the local police department received numerous complaints about the animals having been killed instead of captured. Bengal tigers are obviously one of the most endangered species of mammal in the world, and 18 of them is a decent percentage of all the living wild Bengals on Earth, but if they're deemed a danger to the public, they're still going to be killed. Is it fair? No, I don't think it is. It's not the animals' fault that Terry Thompson set them free. But apparently capturing them proved very difficult, and the primary responsibility of law enforcement officers is public safety. Any animal that's known to have killed a human will be euthanized, at least in the U.S. In Alaska, it's illegal to kill grizzlies without a permit, but the one that killed Timothy Treadwell and Amie Huegenard was still killed. However, I'm pretty sure you as a private citizen are not allowed to go out and start randomly blasting away at grizzly bears if a grizzly killed a family member. Self defense is one thing, hunting down an animal is another, and that's usually left to the authorities to handle.

Name: Amy Christa Ernano
Question: If someone should rent an apartment that's intended for a non-smoker, is it okay if their friends come over and happen to smoke? That's allowed of course, so not to be rude to your guest.
Answer: First of all, even as a longtime smoker (who switched to vaping last year), nobody smokes in my home, whether or not it's allowed by the landlord. Cigarette smoke stinks, especially once it's in your upholstery and curtains and rugs and goes stale, and even in apartments in which smoking isn't forbidden, you can be charged for repainting or replacing carpeting damaged by smoke. (It's also rude to any upstairs neighbors who don't smoke, because they WILL smell it.) I also won't have my pets inhaling secondhand smoke, as rabbits and guinea pigs have sensitive respiratory systems. If I don't smoke in my own home, I'm damn sure not going to let anyone else do it. My current lease forbids smoking anywhere on the property, and guests in my home need to respect that. The only person I see regularly who smokes is my sister (who doesn't smoke much anyway), and she wouldn't dream of even asking if she could smoke in my place. The bottom line is, check your lease. If it says no smoking, that means no smoking, whether it's you or a guest. Are you really willing to risk eviction because you don't want to tell guests to go outside if they need a smoke that badly?

Question: Do some girls bully other girls because they are prettier than them, or because they have better boyfriends?
Answer: Michele “Missy” Avila was actually murdered by her two so-called best friends strictly because she was prettier and more popular than they were, and they were jealous of her. Karen Severson had been best friends with Missy since they were 8 years old, but after they hit puberty, Missy blossomed, while Karen did not. Further complicating things, when they were juniors at San Fernando High School in Los Angeles, Karen began dating Missy's ex-boyfriend, a boy named Randy, and while still dating Karen, Randy tried to get back together with Missy. Missy told Karen, and advised her to dump Randy, but Karen instead took out her anger on Missy. In October of 1985, when the girls were 17, Karen and another friend, Laura Doyle, made plans to hang out with Missy after school. But Missy never came home, and Doyle later called Missy's house looking for her, claiming that she had dropped Missy off to talk to some boys in a Chevy Camaro before going to get gas. Laura said when she returned after getting gas, Missy, the boys, and the Camaro were gone. This was a lie — an elaborate ruse to throw suspicion off of her and Karen. The two, along with another friend, Eva Chirumbolo, had brought Missy into the mountains, where Laura and Karen beat her, cut off her hair, and drowned her in shallow water. Following the murder, and during the investigation, Karen even moved in with Missy's family, feigning support, when what she really wanted was to stay informed on the case. It was Eva — who was not involved in Missy's murder, and was initially threatened into silence by the other two — who ultimately told the police, leading the two girls to be apprehended. Severson and Doyle were each convicted of second degree murder, and sentenced to 15 years to life. Karen was paroled in 2011 after serving 21 years, and Laura was paroled the following year. Question: Could a song like The Wanderer recorded by Dion in 1961 reaching number 2 on the Billboard charts in 1962 be a hit today?
Answer: Maybe if Justin Bieber covered it and it was reworked as a pop song. Otherwise, no. “The Wanderer" is a rock and roll song, and rock and roll is essentially dead. It's a great song, but it's very much of its time, and the teens who were the song's target audience in 1962 are in their 70s now. I love the song, but I'm almost 50 years old, and it was all over the oldies stations when I was a kid in the 80s. Get it? It was an oldie 40 years ago. Shit, even Dion isn't making music that sounds like that anymore (although he is still making music, even at age 83). Because Dion knows that times change, and tastes change with them. That's why he's still making music people are listening to.
